narration:
The organiser is a broad, grey-haired woman with ink on her thumb and a ledger tucked under one arm. She hears you out to the last word without blinking, then pins a fresh notice to the board.

"Free," she says. "Now." She taps the tack in with her thumb. "Lad, the last *hero* who passed through here took three silver off the miller up front, to clear the wolves out of his weir. That was in spring. The miller's still waiting, and so are the wolves."

She turns to face you properly. She isn't hostile, just very hard to impress.

"Nobody gets paid up front on my board. Not heroes, not my own nephew. You get paid when the work's done and someone I trust says it's done." She runs a finger down the ledger. "But if you want the best-paid job, here it is. The spring flood shifted the marker stakes on the Fennick causeway, and the salt carter won't take his wagon across without someone who can find the true road. Thirty silver on delivery at Brindle Ford. Two days there, if the ground holds."

Her eyes drop for a moment to the compass at your belt, then come back up.

"That's the offer. My name's Marta Hollin. I don't do discounts, and I don't do favours for strangers. Not yet, anyway."

narration:
The notice board falls behind you, its papers curling in the wet. Rain comes down steady and cold, and the only warm light on the street spills from a low stone building with a lantern swinging over the door. The painted sign shows a ladle crossed with a key: **the Ladle & Key**.

Inside it smells of peat smoke, wet wool and something with onions in it. A handful of drinkers sit near the hearth. Two of them are drovers, still muddy to the knee. They glance at you and go back to their cups. You shake out your cloak by the door, and the rain spatters across the flagstones.

Behind the bar a broad woman with her sleeves rolled to the elbow is wiping out a pot. She takes in your boots, your cloak and your empty hands, all in one look.

"Hot?" She nods toward a black kettle-pot on a hook by the fire. "Barley and mutton, last of it. Two coppers a bowl, bread included. Ale's one. Kitchen shuts when that pot's scraped, so don't think about it too long."

She sets down the pot. "And if you mean hot as in *news*, the river's up over the causeway, and the ferryman won't cross in the dark. So half the road's sleeping in my common room tonight, and old Bramwell the carter is in the corner cursing it." She jerks her chin toward a grey-bearded man hunched over a cold pipe. "Says he'll pay anyone who knows the high track round the marsh. Nobody here does."

She looks back at you, eyebrows raised. "So. Stew?"

narration:
The innkeeper is nearest, and she doesn't stop wiping the pot while you ask. "Honest work." She looks you over again, longer this time. "This week the honest work is mostly mud. Once the water drops there'll be fence-mending and ditch-clearing from here to the mill. Brask the ferryman will want hands to drag his landing stage back out of the reeds, and he pays in silver if he's in a good mood. He hasn't been in a good mood since spring."

One of the drovers by the hearth snorts into his cup. "Grazier up at Holloway lost a dozen ewes to the flood. He'll pay for anyone who finds them alive. Or dead, so he can stop wondering."

"That's next week's work, though." The innkeeper sets the pot down and folds her arms. "Tonight's work is in that corner."

The old carter has heard every word. He takes the cold pipe out of his teeth and points the stem at the window, where rain is hissing down the glass.

"First light," Bramwell says to the whole room, loud and sour. "I'm going at first light, guide or no guide. Damn this rain. Damn that river. Damn the high track and whoever forgot to put a road on it." He clamps the pipe back in his teeth. "Cheese won't wait for the weather to apologise."

The innkeeper's eyes come back to you, and to your empty hands. "And if you've no coin for stew, I've a woodpile out back that wants splitting and a pot that wants scrubbing. Same price."

narration:
A broad young man in a sweat-dark smock sits on an upturned salt crate by the board, rolling his shoulders like he's itching for an audience. "Nobody in this square's put my back in the dirt since harvest," he tells anyone listening. "Not the smith, not the drover, not the drover's mule."

When you step up, he grins and stands. He's a head shorter than you and twice as wide, with the thick neck and forearms of someone who carries sacks for a living. "Ferrin," he says, and spits in his palm. "First one flat on his back loses. No eye-gouging. Marta, you watching?"

"I'm always watching," Marta says, without looking up from her ledger.

A few carters wander over. Someone draws a ring in the dust with a heel. Ferrin crouches low and waits for you to come to him.

narration:
The ford road narrows between a drainage ditch and a low bank. Behind you, the square’s lamplight fades; ahead, reeds crowd the road where it slopes toward running water.

You keep your pace measured, watching the gaps between the stems. The water’s steady noise could cover a quiet footstep.

“Mind the left edge.”

The voice comes from scarcely six paces away. Only when a man rises from behind a clump of reeds do you distinguish him from the bank. He has seen you first.

He lifts a shuttered lantern. Its light catches a long wooden pole, muddy boots, and a bite of collapsed earth beside the road.

“Lost that bit of bank yesterday. Looks solid in the dark.”

Beyond him, water slides over the ford’s broad paving stones. He stays beside the verge rather than blocking your path.

“Crossing, are you?”

narration:
Marta Hollin stops writing. She lifts her pen off the page, and for a moment the whole square seems to wait with her.

"Her," she says. "Not *his*. And no."

She shuts the ledger over one finger to keep her place. "There's no key, lad. It's a board. It has tacks in it. Anyone who can read can read it, and anyone who can't asks me." She glances down at her belt, where a plain leather purse hangs, then back at you. "And that's my money. Asking for it in front of witnesses, in daylight, has a name round here. It isn't 'hero.'"

Behind you, the carters who stayed to watch the wrestling have stopped talking. Ferrin is still brushing dust off his smock. He doesn't step forward, but he stops brushing, and he doesn't look like he's joking anymore.

Marta doesn't call anyone over. She doesn't need to.

"Here's how it goes," she says, in the same unhurried voice. "You walk off now, sleep off whatever this is, and you're at Oswin Tarrow's wagon at first light, sober and civil. Then the causeway job's still yours, and I'll forget I heard this. Or you keep at it, and I send word to Oswin tonight that he'd do better crossing alone."

She opens the ledger again and finds her line.

"Your choice. I've got work to do."
